REVIEW
Can generative AI reliably synthesise literature? exploring
hallucination issues in ChatGPT
Amr Adel1,2 · Noor Alani2
Received: 23 March 2025 / Accepted: 24 May 2025 / Published online: 21 June 2025
© The Author(s) 2025
Abstract
This study evaluates the capabilities and limitations of generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, in conducting systematic literature reviews. Using the PRISMA methodology, we analysed 124 recent studies, focusing in-depth on a subset of 40 selected
through strict inclusion criteria. Findings show that ChatGPT can enhance efficiency, with reported workload reductions
averaging around 60–65%, though accuracy varies widely by task and context. In structured domains such as clinical research,
title and abstract screening sensitivity ranged from 80.6% to 96.2%, while precision dropped as low as 4.6% in more interpretive tasks. Hallucination rates reached 91%, underscoring the need for careful oversight. Comparative analysis shows that
AI matches or exceeds human performance in simple screening but underperforms in nuanced synthesis. To support more

1  Introduction
Generative artificial intelligence models such as ChatGPT
have attracted growing interest for their potential to automate critical aspects of academic research (Anghelescu et al.
2023). These models are capable of processing and summarising large volumes of text, offering unprecedented speed
and efficiency in handling tasks, such as literature reviews,
data extraction, and synthesis (Alharbi & Asiri 2024). Their
ability to produce structured, coherent outputs has led to
their increasing adoption in research environments that prioritise scalability and rapid knowledge synthesis (García-
López et al. 2025). However, despite these promises, concerns

their increasing adoption in research environments that prioritise scalability and rapid knowledge synthesis (García-
López et al. 2025). However, despite these promises, concerns remain regarding the reliability and factual accuracy
of outputs generated by large language models (Ray 2023)
A key challenge facing generative AI in research applications is the phenomenon of hallucination, where models
generate information that is plausible in form but factually
inaccurate, misleading, or unsupported by source material
(Huang et al. 2025). Hallucinated outputs can include fabricated references, misquoted findings, or incorrect interpretations, each of which poses a direct threat to the integrity
of academic work (Fui-Hoon Nah et al. 2023). These risks
are particularly acute in systematic literature reviews, which
depend on transparent, reproducible, and verifiable methods to identify, screen, and synthesise evidence (Mehrnaz
Mostafapour et al. 2024). An AI system that introduces
errors at any stage of the review process risks propagating
inaccuracies into research syntheses that inform policy decisions, clinical guidelines, and future investigations (Oviedo-

that introduces
errors at any stage of the review process risks propagating
inaccuracies into research syntheses that inform policy decisions, clinical guidelines, and future investigations (Oviedo-
Trespalacios et al. 2023).
This study provides an empirical evaluation of Chat-
GPT’s performance in conducting systematic literature
reviews, with a particular focus on its accuracy, sensitivity,
and propensity for hallucination across key review tasks.
By systematically analysing outputs generated by the model
and comparing them with established review criteria, this
research seeks to identify patterns of strength and limitation in AI-assisted synthesis. The findings aim to inform

2  Methodology
2.1  Application of PRISMA for systematic literature
review
This study adhered to the PRISMA guidelines for systematic
literature review, including study identification, screening,
eligibility assessment, and inclusion (Syriani et al. 2023).
In addition, we propose the Systematic Research Processing Framework (SRPF) as a complementary process model
to enhance AI–human collaboration during review stages.
SRPF is proposed as a conceptual augmentation of the
PRISMA process by integrating AI-assisted tools while
maintaining the reporting standards and methodological
rigor prescribed by PRISMA.

3  Literature review
The emergence of ChatGPT has prompted debate over its
suitability for academic workflows, particularly in systematic literature reviews. Across recent studies, its performance
has been assessed in areas, such as query formulation,
document screening, comparative synthesis, and academic
communication.
3.1  AI utility and limitations in systematic reviews
ChatGPT demonstrates utility in early stage screening and
search tasks, especially in well-structured domains. Studies
report reduced manual workload and faster processing (see
Sect. 6), though performance declines when tasks require
interpretive depth or nuanced judgement. Alaniz et al.
(2023) and Reed and Barnett (2024) found that ChatGPT
can generate complex Boolean queries, particularly when
users provide tailored prompts. However, the effectiveness

3.2  Clinical accuracy and contextual constraints
In medical contexts, ChatGPT has been used to respond to
patient queries and generate clinical summaries, with results
described as generally coherent but occasionally lacking
critical specificity (Gudimella Tirumala et al. 2023; Bulck
& Moons 2023). Al-Sharif et al. (2024) compared ChatGPT
and Bard in oculoplastic scenarios, finding ChatGPT more
fluent but prone to oversimplification underscoring the risk
of AI-generated misinformation in sensitive domains. While
GPT-4 shows notable improvements over GPT-3.5 in areas
such as radiology and orthodontics (Nguyen et al. 2023;
Demir et al. 2024), performance inconsistencies persist,

3.3  Comparative accuracy and hallucination risks
Multiple studies have benchmarked ChatGPT against other
AI tools and human reviewers. It frequently outperforms
competitors like ChatSonic in structured queries (Gudimella
Tirumala et al. 2023), but its performance diminishes when
faced with nuanced or high-risk content, such as nutritional
guidance (Mishra et al. 2024). Accuracy remains inconsistent when the task demands critical appraisal or synthesis, as
noted by Mostafapour et al. (2024) and Hesam Mahmoudi
et al. (2024), who found hallucinations and omissions common during complex data extraction. Although GPT-4 demonstrates higher sensitivity than GPT-3.5 in title and abstract
screening (Matsui et al. 2024), the persistence of hallucination rates (Chelli et al. 2024) underscores a continuing need
for rigorous human oversight.

3.4  Cross‑disciplinary patterns and limitations
Beyond healthcare, ChatGPT supports academic tasks
in education and engineering. It has shown promise in
academic writing and content generation (Quiroz-Martínez
et al. 2024), though challenges with originality detection and
academic integrity remain (Liu et al. 2023). Yıldız (2023,
2024) further observes performance fluctuations across disciplines, indicating that context-specific fine-tuning is essential for reliable integration. Taken together, the literature
suggests that while ChatGPT excels in syntactic fluency and
speed, its epistemic reliability remains domain-dependent,
reinforcing the importance of human intervention and taskspecific configuration in academic settings (Fig. 1).

5  The SRPF framework: a conceptual
response to observed limitations
To address these challenges and enhance the scope of the
systematic review, alternative data collection methods were
employed (Suppadungsuk 2023; Souifi et al. 2025). First,
grey literature sources such as preprints, technical reports,
and white papers were complemented to supplement the
peer-reviewed studies. This allowed for breadth and depth
perspectives on AI-assisted literature reviews, capturing insights from industry practitioners and independent
researchers (Yip et al. 2024).
Second, cross-referencing bibliographies of highly relevant studies helped identify additional sources that were
not retrieved in the initial database searches. This backward snowballing approach ensured that seminal works and
foundational papers were not overlooked. In addition, expert
consultations with AI and literature review specialists were
conducted to validate key findings and uncover studies that
might have been missed in automated searches.
Finally, manual verification of AI-generated references
was

conducted to validate key findings and uncover studies that
might have been missed in automated searches.
Finally, manual verification of AI-generated references
was performed to filter out potentially fabricated citations,
a known issue in AI-driven text generation (Reed & Barnett 2024). This ensured that only authentic and verifiable
sources were included in the analysis. By integrating these
alternative approaches, the study maximised the reliability
and comprehensiveness of its literature review findings.
The Systematic Research Processing Framework (SRPF),
illustrated in Fig. 9, provides a structured workflow integrating human oversight with AI capabilities across four stages:
research kickoff, abstract screening, full-text analysis, and
thematic synthesis. It embeds validation checkpoints and
clarifies task division between AI and researchers, enabling
efficiency without compromising rigour.

6.1  AI strengths in structured review tasks
ChatGPT exhibited strong performance in structured tasks,
such as title and abstract screening, especially when using
GPT-4. Reported sensitivity ranged from 80.6% to 96.5%
(Matsui et al. 2024; Tran et al. 2024), and one study reported
a 99% negative predictive value (Issaiy et al. 2024), indicating reliable exclusion of irrelevant studies. These gains
were consistently associated with refined, domain-specific
prompts, reinforcing the importance of prompt design in
determining outcome quality.
However, precision varies widely. Article screening tasks
revealed precision rates as low as 4.6% (Sanii et al. 2023),
while others reported up to 88% (Alshami et al. 2023). In a
direct comparison, GPT-4 achieved 13.4% precision in article screening versus 9.4% for GPT-3.5 (Chelli et al. 2024),
showing modest but measurable improvement. Nevertheless,
hallucination remained a critical concern. Chelli et al. (2024)
reported hallucination rates between 28 and 91%, highlighting the model’s tendency to fabricate plausible-sounding
references or facts.

6.2  Efficiency and time gains
Four studies reported notable reductions in review time. In
one case, AI completed screening within an hour, whereas
human reviewers required 7–10 days (Issaiy et al. 2024).
Another study noted a 40% reduction in work time, from
100 h to 60 using AI-assisted tools (Ouarhim et al. 2024).
These efficiency gains were most evident in tasks, such as
data extraction and relevance filtering. However, the lack
of standardised reporting made comparisons across studies difficult, and some studies cautioned that time savings
might conceal losses in subtle judgement or information
depth (Jensen et al. 2025).
6.3  Comparative trends across models and tasks
Performance varied significantly across model versions and
task types. GPT-4 consistently outperformed GPT-3.5 and
ChatGPT 3.5 in screening accuracy (Matsui et al. 2024;
Demir et al. 2024). In medical and dental fields, GPT-4’s
structured outputs and improved sensitivity were well-suited
to established terminologies (Nguyen et al. 2023). However,

Of the studies comparing AI to human reviewers, 8
reported comparable performance, 3 found AI underperformed, and 2 noted superior AI performance in recall or
speed (Gudimella Tirumala et al. 2023; Akinseloyin et al.
2023). Nonetheless, across all cases, AI systems require
supervision. Misinterpretation of inclusion criteria (Matsui
et al. 2024), low specificity (Michie et al. 2024), and exclusion of borderline-relevant studies (Chen et al. 2025) were
common issues. In one study, ChatGPT fabricated a convincing but non-existent RCT during a gastroenterology review,
which was only identified through human verification.

Studies also warned of biases embedded in training data

6.5  Refinement through human feedback
Several studies found that ChatGPT's performance improved
with iterative human input. Prompt adjustments, task clarification, and structured output formats reduced hallucinations
and increased relevance (Reed & Barnett 2024; Alaniz et al.
2023). This suggests that effective integration of AI tools
depends not just on the model version but on adaptive human
oversight and prompt design. Where teams employed structured feedback loops, outputs became more reliable over
time.

In conclusion, ChatGPT has demonstrated clear value
in accelerating parts of the SLR workflow, particularly in
screening and data extraction. However, its effectiveness is
shaped by model choice, task structure, and human interaction. High hallucination rates, inconsistency in interpretive tasks, and persistent dependency on expert supervision
underline the need for hybrid review models, where AI augments but does not replace human critical judgement.
7  Discussion
The following discussion interprets these results in the context of generative AI’s potential and limitations in conducting systematic literature reviews. We explore the implications for research practice, challenges of hallucination, and
the necessity for hybrid human–AI review models.
The present investigation provides a nuanced and comprehensive evaluation of ChatGPT’s capability in conducting systematic literature reviews, revealing considerable promise balanced by inherent limitations. Across
the analysis of 124 studies, with an in-depth review of
the top 40 most relevant papers, findings clearly delineate

ChatGPT’s utility in streamlining routine review tasks,
such as title and abstract screening, data extraction, and
preliminary literature synthesis. Specifically, the efficiency
metrics quantified across studies demonstrate substantial time savings, ranging between 40 to 90% (Ouarhim
et al. 2024; Issaiy et al. 2024), significantly accelerating
review workflows compared to traditional methods. For
instance, Issaiy et al. (2024) observed impressive sensitivities ranging from 80.6% to 96.2% in title and abstract
screening tasks performed by GPT-4, a clear indication
of ChatGPT’s potential for efficiency gains. Hallucination
remains a major limitation, with reported rates up to 91%
in some tasks.

to interpret complex logical structures or nuanced scholarly
debates. Studies such as Khraisha et al. (2023) and Akinseloyin et al. (2023) documented considerable struggles in
AI accurately assessing relevance when faced with intricate
logical criteria, suggesting significant reliance on human

Our review also uncovered disparities between AI-driven
and human-led synthesis processes. While ChatGPT typically accelerated tasks, human researchers maintained superiority in accuracy and comprehensive contextual understanding, particularly in full-text evaluations and nuanced
methodological assessments. Michie et al. (2024), for example, found sensitivity ranges of 82–100%, indicating competitive performance with human reviewers, yet even in these
instances, human expertise was crucial for verifying AIgenerated conclusions and preventing erroneous exclusions.

To contextualise the empirical findings, it is essential to
consider how generative AI intersects with broader theoretical debates about trust, governance, and the social role
of technology. O’Neill’s (2022) concept of epistemic trust
emphasises that credibility in knowledge systems depends
not only on clarity or fluency but also on transparency and
verifiability. ChatGPT’s tendency to produce hallucinated
references or unverifiable claims, while linguistically polished, creates a façade of trust that may erode scholarly rigour when left unchecked.
Algorithmic accountability, as described by Pasquale
(2015), is another critical lens. The opacity of large language
models makes it difficult to trace decision-making processes
or assign responsibility when

accountability, as described by Pasquale
(2015), is another critical lens. The opacity of large language
models makes it difficult to trace decision-making processes
or assign responsibility when outputs mislead. This challenges traditional standards of academic accountability,
where authorship and evidence can be scrutinised and cited.
Jasanoff’s (2004) theory of sociotechnical imaginaries
further explains the broader institutional enthusiasm for
integrating AI into academic workflows. These imaginaries privilege speed, automation, and innovation, often at the
expense of critical oversight, human interpretive judgment,
and reflexivity. Recognising this helps reframe AI integration not as a neutral technological advance, but as a valueladen shift in how knowledge is produced, validated, and
governed.
8  Conclusion and future research directions
This study presents a comprehensive evaluation of Chat-
GPT's capacity to enhance systematic literature reviews.
Results indicate that generative AI models can substantially
improve efficiency, with time savings of up to 40% across
various review tasks. Accuracy was particularly strong in
structured fields such as medical research, where

AI models can substantially
improve efficiency, with time savings of up to 40% across
various review tasks. Accuracy was particularly strong in
structured fields such as medical research, where title and
abstract screening sensitivities ranged from 80.6% to 96.2%.
However, performance declined in more interpretative contexts, with precision dropping as low as 4.6% and hallucination rates reaching 91%. These findings underscore the
value of AI–human collaboration, where human oversight is
essential to ensure methodological rigour and prevent misinformation in academic synthesis.
Most reviewed studies recommend hybrid human–AI
models, underscoring collaborative frameworks as optimal for ensuring research accuracy and integrity. Spillias
et al. (2024) effectively demonstrate that hybrid models
leveraging human oversight significantly enhance accuracy
and reliability compared to standalone AI tools. Similarly,
Wang et al. (2024) suggest employing large language model
ensembles to maximise accuracy and reduce hallucination
risks, particularly in systematic reviews across diverse disciplines. Alaniz et al. (2023) and Chen and Feng (2024)
emphasise the necessity of clearly structured

accuracy and reduce hallucination
risks, particularly in systematic reviews across diverse disciplines. Alaniz et al. (2023) and Chen and Feng (2024)
emphasise the necessity of clearly structured prompts and
continuous human supervision, advocating for standardised
guidelines to mitigate methodological disparities across different research contexts.
Future studies should address existing limitations
through several targeted research avenues. First, efforts
should be directed toward enhancing ChatGPT's ability to
handle complex logical structures and nuanced academic
debates, possibly through domain-specific fine-tuning and
enhanced training data sets. Second, future work could
focus on establishing standardised evaluation frameworks
